title: Technical Q&A, mid level data scientist, average answers

questions.text: How do you design a feature pipeline so that training and serving use the same logic?
How do you decide a model is good enough to ship?
How would you detect data drift in production?
When would you pick a simple model over a deep model?
Explain cross validation, and when it can mislead.
How would you explain precision and recall to a product manager?

persona.pushback_style: asks for the specific case behind a general answer

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Selin, thanks for joining. I'm Victor, a machine learning engineer. This is a thirty minute technical conversation. Questions are spoken, with no coding.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Victor, thanks for having me.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What kind of models does your team work on?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We work on churn and demand forecasting models for a retail company. I have been there four years.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. I'll ask about four questions on pipelines, evaluation and monitoring, and then leave time for yours.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you design a feature pipeline so that training and serving use the same logic?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We try to put the feature code in one shared library, so both the training job and the serving service import it. That way the logic is the same. We also test it. We have had some issues with differences before, so we are careful.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What went wrong in one of those past issues?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: One time the training job filled missing values with the mean, but serving filled with zero. Scores were off for about 3 percent of customers. I found it by comparing a sample of features from both sides, and I moved the filling into the shared code.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide a model is good enough to ship?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We look at the metrics on the validation set and compare them to the current model. If it is better, we do an A/B test. If the A/B test is good, we ship. We also check with the product team.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What if the new model is better on the metric but costs more to run?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Then we would talk about it. It depends on how much better it is. If the gain is small, maybe it is not worth it. We could also try making the model smaller.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How would you detect data drift in production?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We would monitor the input features and compare their distributions to training. There are statistical tests like the KS test or the population stability index. If the distance is above a threshold we raise an alert, and maybe retrain.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you set the threshold, and what happens if it is too sensitive?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: On our demand model I used a PSI of 0.2 as the alert level, which is common. At first we got about ten alerts a week, mostly noise. I raised it for seasonal features and added a seven day average, and alerts dropped to two a week.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Last one. When would you pick a simple model over a deep model?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: When the data is small or tabular, and when people need to understand the predictions. For our churn model, a gradient boosted model was within one point of AUC of a neural net, and much easier to explain and run.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How does the team share model work between projects?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: We keep shared feature code in one repository and hold a short model review every two weeks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Selin, the recruiter will contact you within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Victor. Good talking with you.

notes: Average for mid: mostly right but shallow first answers, with no numbers or trade-offs until probed.
